fixes.explanation: Good guess, but the king never shows up in this verse. Isaiah says the woe is for those who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left (Isaiah 5:8). That's the point the verse names. Then they live alone in the land.

Rain isn't in this verse at all, friend. Isaiah says they add house to house and join field to field until no place is left (Isaiah 5:8). That's the point the verse names. And then they live alone in the land.

That's it. Isaiah says they disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands (Isaiah 5:12). The lyre, harp, tambourines, flutes and wine are all at their feasts. Those are the feasts where they miss it.

City guards are a fair guess, but they never show up in this verse. Isaiah says these partiers disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands (Isaiah 5:12). That's what they miss. The music and the wine are what the verse puts at their feasts.
Right, it's Zion's. Isaiah says down go Zion's nobles and masses, her revelers and carousers (Isaiah 5:14). Nobles and masses are both named. They go down together.

Egypt is a big name in the Bible, but it's not here. Isaiah says down go Zion's nobles and masses, her revelers and carousers (Isaiah 5:14). The verse names Zion's people, not Egypt's. Nobles and masses are both on the list.

Babylon is a fair guess for a prophet's warning, but not this time. Isaiah says it's Zion's nobles and masses, her revelers and carousers, who go down (Isaiah 5:14). The verse names Zion's people, not Babylon's. Nobles and masses are both on the list.
The faithful aren't named in this verse. Isaiah says mankind will be brought low, each man humbled, and the arrogant will lower their eyes (Isaiah 5:15). The arrogant are the group the verse names.
Silenced isn't in this verse. Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts will be exalted by His justice (Isaiah 5:16). Exalted means lifted high. And the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness.

That's right. Isaiah says strangers will feed in the ruins of the wealthy (Isaiah 5:17). The verse also says lambs will graze as in their own pastures. Strangers are the ones feeding in what's left of the wealthy's places.

Yes. They say, “Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it!” (Isaiah 5:19). Notice the verse before it is a woe for those who pull sin along with cart ropes (Isaiah 5:18). Those are the ones asking for the show to start.
That's right. Isaiah says woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight (Isaiah 5:21). The wisdom and the cleverness are in their own eyes. That's what this woe names.

The king isn't named in this verse. Isaiah says woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight (Isaiah 5:21). The eyes in question are their own. That's what this woe names.

Elders are a fair guess, but they're not in this verse. Isaiah says woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight (Isaiah 5:21). The eyes in question are their own. That's what this woe names.

Yes, the guilty. Isaiah says they acquit the guilty for a bribe (Isaiah 5:23). The same verse says they deprive the innocent of justice. When a bribe is involved, that's not justice, that's a price tag.
That's right. Isaiah says, “Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.” (Isaiah 5:25). It's a heavy line. The anger is still burning and the hand is still upraised.

Yes, He whistles. Isaiah says He lifts a banner for the distant nations and whistles for those at the ends of the earth (Isaiah 5:26). No letter and no trumpet are in this verse. A banner goes up, a whistle goes out, and then Isaiah says, “Behold—how speedily and swiftly they come!”

A trumpet is a good guess, but this verse doesn't mention one. Isaiah says He lifts a banner for the distant nations and whistles for those at the ends of the earth (Isaiah 5:26). A banner goes up, and a whistle goes out.

Not quite. Isaiah says none of them grows weary or stumbles, and no belt is loose and no sandal strap is broken (Isaiah 5:27). Loose belts and broken sandal straps are exactly what the verse says they don't have. The verse also says no one slumbers or sleeps.
That's right. Isaiah says no belt is loose and no sandal strap is broken (Isaiah 5:27). He adds that none of them grows weary or stumbles. No one slumbers or sleeps, either.

The king isn't named in this verse. Isaiah says they growl and seize their prey, and they carry it away, and no one can rescue it (Isaiah 5:29). "No one" is a big phrase. It leaves out every rescuer, a king included.
